title: Day 1 · Phase 1 — Overview, safety zones, theme commit
bodyHtml:
DAY 1 · Phase 1 — Overview, safety, theme

Walk the corridor; meet the four hazard zones; commit a team theme.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS (preview)

K1. Four components of a DC circuit. K2. Energy chain preview. K4. Veer cause preview.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: The asteroid study has supplied models of motion, forces, energy, and circuits. Students now apply those models to a real, low-voltage model vehicle, using the actual build constraints and supervised tools.

How today connects:

Use today’s build, test, or design decision to apply the course physics. Support the claim with a measurement or a labeled model; state where the comparison with an engineered asteroid response stops.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hand out packets. Frame the unit: "For 9 days you'll build a car. Day 9 you race it AND write a transfer task defending three physics choices."

5–15 min

• Walk the actual race corridor. Students stand in it. Notice the width. Notice what a 2-cm veer does over 6 m. The corridor IS the design constraint.

15–25 min

• Vocabulary preview (battery, switch, motor, series, current) — named, not defined yet. Project the parts kit.

25–40 min

• Four safety zones: soldering iron, hot glue, drill, switch installation. Show, don't explain. Each subsequent day opens with a 60-second beat on the relevant zone.

40–48 min

• Team formation (3–4 per team) + theme commitment. Teams write theme + biggest expected physical challenge on packet exit ticket.

48–50 min

• Marzano 1-2-3 conversation on K1/K2/K4 preview.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Ask each student to identify a corridor constraint and explain how it affects a design choice. Check the safety demonstration before tool access; a completed theme alone is not physics evidence.

Formative check: exit-ticket completeness; theme clear enough for a stranger to recognize.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: packets printed; corridor cleared; one parts kit per team staged on tables; safety reference page open.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no new reading. Honors: no new reading. Use the project packet and prior course references as needed during preparation.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §22.8 Torque on a Current Loop: Motors and Meters (pp. 1048–1051); §20.4 Electric Power and Energy (pp. 939–942). Focus: Trace energy from the low-voltage source through the motor to the car; the project packet governs tools and build safety. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Differentiation: ELs — pair theme commitments with a sentence frame; SWDs — give team-role assignment cards (build lead, safety, scribe).

CPA teaching sequence: Show the build step, identify its physics on a labeled sketch, and rehearse the tool procedure under supervision. Use measured values in a structured table; each student explains a choice before the team continues.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 2 · Phase 1 — PhET circuit + soldering practice
bodyHtml:
DAY 2 · Phase 1 — Simulate it, then practice the iron

Build a working series circuit in PhET; produce a clean scrap solder joint.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K1. Four DC components. K2. Energy chain. S1. Series circuit in PhET. S2. Solder on scrap.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: The asteroid study has supplied models of motion, forces, energy, and circuits. Students now apply those models to a real, low-voltage model vehicle, using the actual build constraints and supervised tools. The preceding meeting focused on Overview, safety zones, theme commit.

How today connects:

Use today’s build, test, or design decision to apply the course physics. Support the claim with a measurement or a labeled model; state where the comparison with an engineered asteroid response stops.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–1 min

• Safety beat: soldering iron.

1–15 min

• PhET Circuit Construction Kit: DC. Teacher demos the loop (battery → switch → bulb stand-in for motor). Students build it. Probe: open the switch, double the voltage, break a wire. Three observations recorded.

15–25 min

• Energy-chain worked example: chemical → electrical → mechanical-rotational → mechanical-translational. Students label each arrow on their packet diagram.

25–40 min

• Scrap solder practice. Two joints turned in. Teacher inspects: shiny, tight, compact.

40–45 min

• Marzano conversation. Quick sketch of the four-link energy chain in their own words.

45–48 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

48–50 min

• Tomorrow: gears, wheels, ratio reasoning, wheel commit.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check a complete circuit and a safe practice joint before the build. Ask each student to explain the switch's role using the circuit diagram.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: PhET loaded on lab computers (offline build is fine); 1 iron per pod with stand; scrap wire + solder; eye protection.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no new reading. Honors: no new reading. Use the project packet and prior course references as needed during preparation.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §20.2 Ohm’s Law: Resistance and Simple Circuits (pp. 931–933); §21.4 DC Voltmeters and Ammeters (pp. 998–1002). Focus: Check the circuit model and measurement connections before supervised soldering; follow the project safety procedure. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves: on first power in PhET — "What did you predict would happen? What did happen?" Make the model-vs-observation move habitual now; it pays off on Day 6.

title: Day 3 · Phase 1 — Mechanical advantage + wheel commit
bodyHtml:
DAY 3 · Phase 1 — The one design decision

Wheel selection: ratio reasoning drives the prediction.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K3. Gear-pair RPM/torque relationship. R1. Ratio reasoning for wheel diameter. R2. Justify wheel choice.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: The asteroid study has supplied models of motion, forces, energy, and circuits. Students now apply those models to a real, low-voltage model vehicle, using the actual build constraints and supervised tools. The preceding meeting focused on PhET circuit + soldering practice.

How today connects:

Use today’s build, test, or design decision to apply the course physics. Support the claim with a measurement or a labeled model; state where the comparison with an engineered asteroid response stops.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–1 min

• Safety beat: hot glue (tomorrow).

1–10 min

• CALLOUT: "The motor only spins. Gears change how." Vocab pass: RPM, gear ratio, torque, circumference, mechanical advantage.

10–22 min

• Worked example 1: 2:1 gear ratio (10-tooth on motor, 20-tooth on axle). Worked example 2: wheel circumference C = π × d.

22–38 min

• Wheel comparison table. Teams measure each candidate wheel pair, compute C, predict relative speed and starting effort vs. the smallest wheel. Ratio reasoning rule: doubling diameter doubles top speed at the same axle RPM AND doubles starting effort.

38–43 min

• Wheel commit. Teams write: "We chose ___-mm wheels because ___; we predict our top speed will be ___ relative to a team that chose ___ because ___."

43–46 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

46–50 min

• Marzano on K3/R1/R2. Tomorrow: chassis cut.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Inspect the wheel and gear calculation with units. Each student should justify the speed-versus-torque tradeoff behind the team's choice.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: sample wheels of each available size at the front; rulers; the 10T motor gear + 20T axle gear shown side by side as the canonical pair.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no new reading. Honors: no new reading. Use the project packet and prior course references as needed during preparation.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §9.5 Simple Machines (pp. 400–404); §6.1 Rotation Angle and Angular Velocity (pp. 245–249). Focus: Compare wheel-and-axle mechanical advantage with rotational speed and rim speed; use the actual gear and wheel dimensions. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves: when students hedge ("we'll just see what works") — "Make a prediction. Day 6 will tell you whether you were right. That's the whole point."

Differentiation: ELs — sentence frame for the prediction; Honors extension — challenge to estimate ABSOLUTE top speed (they'll need to assume a motor RPM, which is the lesson on Day 6).

CPA teaching sequence: Show the build step, identify its physics on a labeled sketch, and rehearse the tool procedure under supervision. Use measured values in a structured table; each student explains a choice before the team continues.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. title: Day 5 · Phase 2 — Axles + alignment (Build steps 4–9)
bodyHtml:
DAY 5 · Phase 2 — The day that decides the race

Axles parallel. Roll-straight ≥3 m unpowered.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K4. Veer cause = friction asymmetry → vertical-axis torque. S4. Parallel axle install.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: The asteroid study has supplied models of motion, forces, energy, and circuits. How today connects:

Use today’s build, test, or design decision to apply the course physics. Support the claim with a measurement or a labeled model; state where the comparison with an engineered asteroid response stops.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–1 min

• Safety beat: hot glue.

1–10 min

• CALLOUT: "Why parallel matters." Top-down sketch of friction asymmetry → torque about a vertical axis through the car. Not a power problem. A geometry problem.

10–35 min

• Build steps 4–9: pen-tube axle holders, drill 3/16" holes along the Day-4 line, slide axles, press-fit wheels, mount the 20T axle gear (slightly offset for motor mesh tomorrow). Roll test #1.

35–42 min

• Adjust. Re-glue. Roll test #2. Data table records distance before veer + what changed.

42–45 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

45–50 min

• Marzano on K4/S4. Teams that did NOT hit 3 m straight: record what they'll adjust before tomorrow's first power-on.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Use a straightness trial to connect measured veer to axle alignment. Ask each student to propose one controlled adjustment and a way to test its effect.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

Materials and setup: pen tubes pre-cut; 3/16" bit; hot glue guns at glue station; corridor available for roll tests.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §5.1 Friction (pp. 212–218). Focus: Use friction and contact-force ideas to explain alignment and rolling losses. Read only the subsection needed for your test result. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves: when a car veers — "Which wheel has more friction? How do you know? What about the geometry would cause that?" Push for the physical cause before the fix.

title: Day 6 · Phase 2 — Gears, motor, switch, FIRST POWER + RPM (Build steps 10–15)
bodyHtml:
DAY 6 · Phase 2 — First power-on + measurement

Wire the loop. Power on. Measure axle RPM. Compare to Day 3 prediction.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K1/K2 reinforced. S5. Switch install without breaking chassis. S6. Measure axle RPM. R1 revisited.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: The asteroid study has supplied models of motion, forces, energy, and circuits. Students now apply those models to a real, low-voltage model vehicle, using the actual build constraints and supervised tools. The preceding meeting focused on Axles + alignment (Build steps 4–9).

How today connects:

Use today’s build, test, or design decision to apply the course physics. Support the claim with a measurement or a labeled model; state where the comparison with an engineered asteroid response stops.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–1 min

• Safety beat: drill + first power-on.

1–25 min

• Build steps 10–15: motor gear, motor mount + mesh, drill switch hole (CHASSIS-BREAK WATCH — wood block under chassis), battery clip, wire battery → switch → motor in series (tape splices for now), direction test.

25–30 min

• Mini-lecture beat: name the wires they just connected. Battery = source. Switch = gate. Motor = load. "Break the loop anywhere, current stops everywhere."

30–42 min

• RPM measurement protocol. Mark 2.00 m. Switch on at start, stopwatch starts. Stop at finish. Compute v = d/t, rev/s = v/C, RPM = (rev/s) × 60. Three runs.

42–45 min

• Comparison cell: predicted Day-3 speed vs. measured Day-6 speed. 1–2 sentence reflection on prediction-vs-observation.

45–48 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

48–50 min

• Marzano on S5/S6.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check the circuit before first power, then compare measured RPM or travel speed with the prediction. Students must name a model assumption that could explain a discrepancy.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: drills with 3/16" bits + wood blocks; tape; stopwatches (or phones); 2-meter tape on the floor; corridor.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no new reading. Honors: no new reading. Use the project packet and prior course references as needed during preparation.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §6.1 Rotation Angle and Angular Velocity (pp. 245–249); §23.6 Back Emf (pp. 1097–1098). Focus: Connect measured RPM with angular and rim speed; use back emf to explain the difference between a running and stalled motor. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on first power-on: teacher prompt before the click — "What direction will the car go? Why?" Right after the click — "What surprised you? What didn't?" Make it the modeling conversation, not a celebration.

Differentiation: ahead → run a second RPM trial with the switch held down only briefly (energy depletion check); behind → teacher pairs to hold stopwatch + record while team focuses on driving.

CPA teaching sequence: Show the build step, identify its physics on a labeled sketch, and rehearse the tool procedure under supervision. Use measured values in a structured table; each student explains a choice before the team continues.

title: Day 8 · Phase 3 — Finish, signature, photo, practice (Build steps 19–23)
bodyHtml:
DAY 8 · Phase 3 — Race-ready

Theme complete. Practice heats. Tomorrow is the race.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S7. Theme execution complete.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: The asteroid study has supplied models of motion, forces, energy, and circuits. Students now apply those models to a real, low-voltage model vehicle, using the actual build constraints and supervised tools. Use today’s build, test, or design decision to apply the course physics. Support the claim with a measurement or a labeled model; state where the comparison with an engineered asteroid response stops.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–1 min

• Safety beat: choose the most relevant zone for the day's work.

1–20 min

• Decoration finish, paint touch-ups, sealant if needed.

20–28 min

• Sign the underside of the chassis with team name + date. Write the name card for tomorrow's judging table.

28–35 min

• Group photoshoot (cars side by side, then individual hero shots).

35–45 min

• Practice runs in the actual corridor. Record practice times. Tune.

45–48 min

Individual transfer plan: Read tomorrow’s three physics prompts. Select your own measured evidence for wheel speed, alignment, and circuit choices. Plan how to explain and defend each choice, and name one useful comparison with a powered asteroid-response system and one limit. Keep the plan in class.

48–50 min

• Marzano on S7. Tomorrow: race + judging + transfer task.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Inspect the recorded practice results and each student's transfer-task plan. Students should identify their own evidence for wheels, alignment, and circuit choices.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

Focus: Select the speed and electrical-energy ideas needed to defend your measured design choices. No new reading during tomorrow's assessment. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on design judging conversation: when teams ask what scores well — "Three things: did you honor your Day-1 theme commitment? Is the finish craftsmanship visible? Is the build craftsmanship visible? Theme + finish + build. The race is its own conversation."

Differentiation: ahead → run a competitor's car too and offer feedback; behind → set a single specific tuning goal (e.g., "reduce veer") and use practice runs to test it.

CPA teaching sequence: Show the build step, identify its physics on a labeled sketch, and rehearse the tool procedure under supervision. Use measured values in a structured table; each student explains a choice before the team continues.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

Use the final practice run as evidence collection for tomorrow’s individual defense. Display the four-dimension rubric during planning; do not supply the assessment explanation.

title: Day 9 · Phase 4 — Race + design judging + transfer task (Build step 24)
bodyHtml:
DAY 9 · Phase 4 — The transfer day

Race in heats. Judge design. Defend three physics choices in writing.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS (load-bearing)

R3. Observation vs. prediction. R4. Three physics choices defended. Final ratings recorded for ALL unit targets.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: The asteroid study has supplied models of motion, forces, energy, and circuits. Students now apply those models to a real, low-voltage model vehicle, using the actual build constraints and supervised tools. The preceding meeting focused on Finish, signature, photo, practice (Build steps 19–23).

How today connects:

Use today’s build, test, or design decision to apply the course physics. Support the claim with a measurement or a labeled model; state where the comparison with an engineered asteroid response stops.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–3 min

• Race format briefed. Heats called. Rubric posted: time + straightness (1-2-3); theme + finish + build (1-2-3).

3–22 min

• Heats. Teacher records time + straightness as each heat runs. Photos.

22–32 min

• Design judging at the table. Teacher (optional peer voting) scores theme execution, finish craftsmanship, build craftsmanship.

32–43 min

Individual transfer task: Use the plan and measurements from Day 8 to defend the packet’s three choices: wheels with computed speed, alignment, and circuit with a counterfactual. Explain one useful comparison with a powered response to 2026-XJ and one limit of the analogy.

43–48 min

Peer defense: Each partner explains one choice and answers a question about its evidence or assumptions. Use Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Each student records a specific feedback note and a brief final revision in their own work.

48–50 min

Submit the individual analysis, defense note, and four-dimension self-rating. Complete the separate target self-rating after the individual work. Teacher ratings follow review of the evidence.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Collect each student's explanation and defense, supported by measured results. Keep race performance and craftsmanship scores separate from evidence of individual physics understanding.

Feedback and revision: Return a separate judgment on each physics dimension. Identify one specific claim, computation, or model limit that needs new evidence; arrange a revision conference within the Unit 1 revision window.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: race corridor marked + cleared; stopwatch; judging table with one slot per team; signed-chassis check before heats.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no new reading. Honors: no new reading. Use the project packet and prior course references as needed during preparation.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: No new OpenStax reading during the transfer assessment. Use only the references permitted in the assessment plan; revisit a focused section after feedback.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on first race surprise: when a car wins that wasn't expected — "Why did this car win? Reason from the physics, not the team." Make the race a thinking artifact, not a competition.

Differentiation on the transfer task: ELs — sentence frames for each of the 3 prompts; SWDs — verbal version of the wheel computation, written version of the other two; ahead → add a 4th prompt on what they'd change next time and why.

Closing: growth chart completed across the unit's 15 targets. Marzano conversation closes the unit and the CPA year.

CPA teaching sequence: Show the build step, identify its physics on a labeled sketch, and rehearse the tool procedure under supervision. Use measured values in a structured table; each student explains a choice before the team continues.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

Assessment conventions: Use the Unit 1 rubric: Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Score the four dimensions independently from 0–4; report the profile without averaging and use the established lowest-dimension conversion. Science checks the physics; Reasoning checks the choice and justification of the model; Communication checks labeled, organized work; Transfer-to-Asteroid checks the supported connection and its limits. Peer and student ratings are feedback; the teacher makes the final judgment. Target self-ratings use the separate 1–3 scale and do not automatically become mastery ratings. Revisions follow Unit 1’s two-week window, with new evidence for a one-level move on a dimension.

Keep the project’s race, straightness, theme, and craftsmanship measures as separate performance criteria. The physics transfer profile uses the Unit 1 dimensions. The vehicle is an analogy for a powered engineered response, not a claim that a classroom car can deflect an asteroid. Provide additional assessment time when an access plan or unfinished defense requires it.
